disposition_reason: Narrative review (Bioversity International / CAF, version 4 Nov 2019) with no new measurements. Its bean-Cd values (Annex 1.2, Section 1) are compilations of other studies and are recorded only as flagged secondary citations; its substantive contribution for the cocoa page is the summarised mitigation evidence (liming, organic amendments, nutrition, microbes, genotype, post-harvest, blending, sourcing), recorded as controls with the original studies named, plus the regulatory overview.
disposition_locator: Executive summary; Section 1 (Tables 1-2, ML_CM equation); Sections 2.2, 3.2.3-3.2.8, 4.3-4.9; Section 5 (mitigation hierarchy); Section 6.2.5 projects P19-P20; Annex 1.2 (p61); Annex 2 (pp62-63)

findings.material: cacao beans
findings.locator: Section 2.2.1, report p9
findings.notes: SECONDARY CITATION: Duplicate of Annex 1.2 Zarcinas row; listed only because the text attributes it to phosphate-fertiliser input (soil P vs Cd R2=0.80). Do not count twice.

controls.outcome: Ramtahal et al. 2018 (Trinidad and Tobago), 3 kg slaked lime/tree: soil pH significantly increased; leaf Cd fell in both limed and untreated trees (p<0.05) but the reduction in limed trees was 3-fold that of untreated. Bean Cd not yet reported. Original study: Ramtahal et al. 2018 (as cited).

Schneider 2016 (Peru), slaked lime low dose 2.5 and 1.85 t/ha, high dose 5.8 and 3.6 t/ha: significant difference in bioavailable soil Cd vs control; bean Cd not measured. Effect size not given in the review.
Zamora 2018 (Peru), dolomite 1.8, 2.7 and 3.6 kg/plant for 12 months: 'significant decrease' in bean Cd reported; control values and sample size not provided, so no effect size available.

controls.comparator: unamended soils, 3 soil types, Cd-spiked, 28 days
controls.outcome: Chavez et al. 2016a: zeolite at 0.5% and 2% did not raise soil pH and did not reduce 0.01 M CaCl2- or Mehlich-3-extractable Cd (null result).

controls.comparator: unamended soil spiked with 5 mg/kg Cd
controls.outcome: Chavez et al. 2016a: vermicompost at 2% effectively reduced CaCl2- and Mehlich-3-extractable soil Cd, possibly via a substantial pH increase; no plant/bean measurement; effect size not given in the review.
Zamora 2018 (Peru), 30, 60 and 90 t/ha: response variable; compost generally reduced bean Cd, chicken manure did not. No numbers given in the review.

Zamora 2018 (Peru), ZnSO4 0.09, 0.18 and 0.27 kg/plant: 'modest decreasing trend' in bean Cd; no numbers. Correlative studies (Argüello 2019; Gramlich 2017; Arévalo-Gardini 2017; Crozier 2012) found higher soil/leaf Zn not associated with lower cacao Cd.
Nereida 2011 (Venezuela), 50 or 150 mg/kg per tree: reduced bioavailable soil Cd; no bean data or effect size given.
Arbulu Zuazo 2017 (Peru): pot trials reduced Cd bioavailability, especially at applications over 5%; field trial underway; no numbers.

Mixed: Ramtahal et al. 2012 commercial mycorrhizal product increased seedling Cd; Jacome et al. 2016 decreased seedling Cd only in soils spiked at 12 and 24 mg/kg; Revoredo et al. 2017 Streptomyces (spiked 100-200 mg/kg) too small to interpret; Pérez Moncada et al. 2019 field experiment with native AMF reduced bean Cd in soil spiked with 24 mg/kg Cd. Spiking levels far exceed typical plantation soils; no effect sizes given.

controls.control: Low-accumulating genotypes as rootstock or scion
controls.outcome: Arévalo-Gardini et al. (unpublished): leaf Cd of seedlings of 60 genotypes in spiked soil ranged 1-10 mg/kg; International Cocoa Genebank (Trinidad) noted bean Cd differences among 100 accessions on similar soils (Lewis et al. 2018); Engbersen et al. 2019 (Honduras, 11 grafted cultivars) significant cultivar differences and no bean-soil Cd relationship; Barraza et al. (in prep.) different soil-to-plant transfer for Nacional vs CCN51. Review considers rootstock/scion reconversion a mid- to long-term solution.

controls.control: Avoid irrigation/flood sources high in Cd and chloride
controls.comparator: farms or soils with different water regimes
controls.outcome: Argüello et al. 2019: Cd bioavailability rose sharply at soil chloride >500 ppm (EC 1:5 about 350 µS/cm); Chavez et al. 2015: bean Cd best predicted by bioavailable Cd plus topsoil EC (R2=0.73); Llatance 2018 (Peru) soil Cd <0.008 non-inundated vs 0.043 inundated vs 0.11 mg/kg semi-inundated; Maurice (pers. comm.) highest bean Cd up to 4.3 mg/kg on regularly flooded farms.

controls.control: Fertiliser choice: low-Cd phosphate and nitrate vs ammonium N
controls.outcome: Sedimentary phosphate rock 1-150 mg/kg Cd (up to 300) vs volcanic 1-4 mg/kg; about 85% of fertiliser phosphate is sedimentary. Zarcinas et al. 2004 (Malaysia) soil P vs Cd R2=0.80 (soil Cd mean 0.11, beans 0.66 mg/kg). Zug et al. 2019 (Peru): N-fertiliser use 'dramatically increased' bean Cd and P fertiliser use modestly positively correlated. No effect sizes given.

controls.control: Soil Mn and tree age as modifiers
controls.outcome: Argüello et al. 2019: bioavailable Mn explained 8% of bean Cd variation in a model with total soil Cd, pH and TOC; Geeroms 2016: Mn:Cd >20:1 associated with lower uptake; Argüello 2019 and Alianza Cacao (unpublished): younger trees absorb more Cd than older ones.

controls.control: Site selection: avoid high-risk areas for new plantations
controls.outcome: Recommends avoiding new plantations in areas known to produce high-Cd cacao; notes soil Cd thresholds (e.g. Peru DS 011-2017-MINAM) are poor predictors because bean Cd can be high on low-Cd soils; suggests digital soil mapping. No quantitative outcome.

Evidence inconclusive: Alianza Cacao (pers. comm.) Cd appears to migrate to the bean surface during fermentation so shell removal may lower nib Cd; Kruszewski et al. 2018 found no decrease after winnowing (Ecuador and Dominican Republic raw cocoa vs chocolate mass from three manufacturers); Mounicou et al. 2003 reported Cd concentration increase through water loss. Review judges post-harvest changes unlikely to reduce Cd substantially without quality effects and useful only for lots marginally above limits.

Unpublished, industry-run: review text reports 20-25% Cd reduction via microbiology (beans) and nanotechnology (cocoa mass), details not available; project P19 (CasaLuker/Los Andes University) micellar bodies on cocoa matrices 10-30% reduction; project P20 (CasaLuker/Agrosavia) Bacillus/Lactobacillus strains, pilot 10-40 kg cocoa mass, 13-28% removal at 12-24 h contact. Sensory impact not reported. Not peer reviewed.
controls.locator: Section 4.9 (p26); Section 6.2.5 projects P19 and P20 (pp49-51)

controls.control: Blending high-Cd with low-Cd beans; fine-scale segregation
controls.outcome: Blending described as an effective short-term route to meet limits but erodes origin identity (fine/flavour cacao about 6% of trade). For unblendable fine cacao, fine-scale sampling to segregate compliant beans before fermentation (Remigio 2014). No numbers.

controls.control: Bean acceptance limits derived from product MLs
controls.outcome: Maximum Cd in cocoa mass ML_CM = ML_product / cocoa-mass fraction; e.g. 0.8 / 0.7 = 1.1 mg/kg for 70% dark chocolate, used as an approximation for beans/nibs. Buyers request bean limits of 0.5-1.1 mg/kg. No accepted bean sampling scheme; suggested analogues: 5 samples per 60 kg sack, or 10 samples per half tonne (one analysis per 50 kg), each sample 1 kg.

regulatory.status: 2018-2025 warning level (not a market ban; products above can be sold with a warning)

contradictions_with_stored_summary: Stored summary lists Arévalo-Gardini et al. 2017 with '57% of samples exceeded 0.8 mg/kg'; the primary says 'nearly 57% of sample sites' (n=70).
Stored summary presents Annex 1.2 values as if they were this report's 'Key numbers' without flagging that all are secondary compilations of other studies with unstated basis and bean/nib form.
Stored summary appends Zug et al. 2019 (mean 2.46, range 0.02-12.5) to the Annex 1.2 list; in the primary it appears only in Section 1 text, not Annex 1.2.
Stored summary classifies the source as 'gov-report'; it is a Bioversity International / CAF (development bank and CGIAR centre) review, not a government report.

Stored summary frontmatter jurisdictions include CO, HN, BO, CR, DO, GH, NG, CM, ID, MY; Annex 1.2 has no Colombia or Costa Rica bean rows (Colombia appears only in projects and Rodríguez Albarracín leaf-litter text).
unresolved: Annex 1.2 secondary rows: originals in corpus only for vitola2016-cocoa-beans-heavy-trace-elements and arevalo-gardini2017-peru-cacao-regional-metals (and possibly ramtahal2016 / barraza2019, which are different papers from Ramtahal 2015 and Barraza 2017 cited here). Argüello 2019, Gramlich 2017/2018, Chavez 2015, Barraza 2017, Kruszewski 2018, Bertoldi 2016, Takrama 2015, Amankwaah 2015, Fauziah 2001, Zarcinas 2004, Assa 2018, Zug 2019 and the grey literature (Mite 2010, Acosta and Pozo 2013, Llatance 2018, Tantalean 2017, Cárdenas 2012) have no wiki/sources page found by slug prefix.
Annex 1.2 footnote says 21 studies, while the table has 30 rows from 21 named studies including duplicate study rows; the two Tantalean et al. 2017 rows are unlabelled.
Mite et al. 2010 is rendered differently here (n=153, 0.32-1.80) and in romero-estevez2019 Table 2 (per-province, n totalling 139, max 4.08); the original congress paper was not checked.
Figure 2 (box plots of means by region) is an image; not digitised (it is derived from Annex 1.2 anyway).

Annex 2 (baseline-study regression directions) is a directional summary with R-squared values only; it was not converted into controls beyond the narrative-cited items because the per-study effect sizes are not given.

Regulatory values are as cited in 2019; the Codex values were drafts at the time (later adopted as CXS 193 MLs per other sources), the FSANZ and Russian entries should be verified against the instruments.
